Processes and prediction forks

How the desktop adapter forwards process requests and composer prediction forks on connected machines, and how throwaway chats stay memory-only.

About 5 min read

Part of the Codex app-server adapter.

The desktop runs git commands (the branch and pull request chips) and terminals on a connected machine through the app-server's process API: process/spawn, process/writeStdin, process/resizePty and process/kill. A process handle belongs to one connection, and output arrives as process/outputDelta and process/exited notifications on that connection. The adapter sends these requests unchanged to that machine's native engine and returns its answer unchanged, as the native app-server does, for the relay and SSH paths alike. Nothing runs in the adapter or in a gateway executor.

Some refusals come from the engine itself and also occur natively. The signed SDK (0.162.0-alpha.17.2) rejects a working directory that is not absolute with -32600 "AbsolutePathBuf deserialized without a base path"; the desktop sends its projectless ~ placeholder when a remote composer has no project. The SDK answers -32603 "failed to spawn process" for a directory that does not exist on that machine, and -32600 "no active process for process handle" when the desktop stops a git command that has already exited. Deleting a chat that never wrote a rollout returns "no rollout found for thread id", which the desktop recognizes.

The desktop's composer suggestions resume a chat and then fork it with experimentalPredictionMode: true, ephemeral: true and excludeTurns: true. Such a fork starts from the loaded parent's effective settings, and the SDK refuses it with -32600 when the request carries any override, even a single config key. The adapter forwards a prediction fork exactly as the desktop sent it to the engine that owns the chat. It adds no restored reasoning, gateway model, provider, catalog or speed tier, applies no hooks-alias correction, and never refuses it over an unknown tier. Before this, the adapter added a native chat's saved reasoning effort to the fork, so every suggestion fork failed. Ordinary gateway forks keep the tier and reasoning handling described above. An ordinary native fork reaches the engine exactly as the desktop sent it, with no model, provider or effort added. One that names no model, such as a side chat, runs the configured default model, and one that names the chat's model without an effort gets the engine's own effort, as natively (native chats keep their model). The change applies to the next adapter connection after an update.

On a gateway chat, a composer prediction fork runs real inference on that chat's provider, so it counts as that provider's usage. In 0.4.0 these forks always failed and ran nothing.

Any ephemeral chat (prediction forks included) is memory-only. Its result writes no reasoning record, no service-tier row and no compaction-recovery row, and a later turn or applied settings change on it writes none either. The adapter keeps only an in-memory route, so a turn started on the chat reaches the owning engine without a service-tier or reasoning write. The newest 256 such chats stay tracked this way, and each one counts toward that cap whether it was started, resumed, forked, or first seen when a turn probed its owner. thread/closed or thread/unsubscribe for one of them forgets its route and chat snapshot at once; a later turn on a chat that is still loaded in the engine is recognized as ephemeral again from the engine's own chat read and stays memory-only.

When the 256 cap pushes a chat out, its route and snapshot go but its id is kept in a second set of the newest 4096 evicted ids, because the engine may still have the chat subscribed. A settings notification for one of those ids writes nothing durable, and neither does the result of a resume of one. A turn that is already running when its chat is closed, unsubscribed or evicted writes no reasoning record when the engine answers.

The private stores have different bounds. The service-tier store holds at most 16384 chats and its file at most 4 MiB (long model names reach that limit first). When a write would pass either limit, it evicts other chats instead of failing: rows that were never stamped with a record time first, then the rows stamped longest ago, and never the chat being written. A chat's row and its unknown-tier marker (below) count as rows, each by its exact size, and leave together (an unknown tier keeps both, so it counts as two rows): chats go oldest first by the newest stamp of either, so an older row never outlives a newer marker. The reasoning store also holds at most 16384 chats and evicts the chat observed longest ago when it is full, but its 4 MiB file limit is a hard one: a write that would pass it is refused rather than making room.

The per-chat compaction overrides that a gateway executor remembers are forgotten when the chat closes or is unsubscribed, deleted or archived. If 4096 chats are still held, remembering another drops the one set longest ago instead of refusing the new chat.

The backends recognize a gateway executor's throwaway chats in three ways: the executor's thread/started notification or the answer to thread/start, thread/resume or thread/fork marks the chat ephemeral, or the request is a thread/fork with experimentalPredictionMode (or a start or fork with ephemeral: true). The turn and token events of such a chat are not written to the on-disk compaction store, which holds the compaction recovery state of every gateway chat, and neither is the reset a thread/rollback would write. A resume never makes a chat throwaway from its own ephemeral flag, so a durable chat resumed with ephemeral: true is saved as usual. The newest 4096 such ids are tracked, and an id is forgotten when its chat is closed, unsubscribed, deleted or archived. The store itself holds at most 4096 chats and 4 MiB. When a write would pass either limit, for a new chat or for an existing chat whose row grows past the byte bound, it drops the chats observed longest ago instead of failing, and never the chat being written, so a full store no longer stops recovery for the other chats.

Each rpc_error event records a fixed rejection name for the refusal, so these cases can be told apart without storing error text; see diagnostics.
